title: Use of Low-Value Cancer Care in Practices Acquired by Private Equity Firms
pub: JNCI: Journal of the National Cancer Institute, published online 30 March 2026
author: Aaron P. Mitchell · Miranda B. Lam · Caroline Carlin · Kevin Tyan · Maryam Mooghali · Ziad Zakaria · Reshma Ramachandran · Jeah Jung

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source concerns private-equity acquisition of oncology practices and low-value cancer treatment use. It provides no evidence or argument about legal AI, jagged capability, verification, selective deployment, or legal-work redesign, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s central distinction between financial incentives and demonstrated patient effects. It finds no increase across five measured low-value cancer treatments—two declined—while limiting the inference to those services and treating the results as associative rather than causal.
qs: PE acquisition was not associated with differences in use of three of the low-value treatments and was associated with reductions in two low-value treatments (GCSF for low-risk chemotherapy and bevacizumab for ovarian cancer).
This study was limited to five low-value cancer treatments and did not analyze other services.

mo.t: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains

kp.k: Private equity incentives motivated scrutiny of oncology care
kp.d: The authors investigate oncology ownership, not AI or legal services. They report that approximately 10% of medical oncologists and 15% of radiation oncologists practiced in PE-owned clinics by 2022, amid limited evidence on utilization and quality. They frame increased low-value treatment as a potential consequence of short-term financial incentives, rather than an established outcome: unnecessary treatments and expensive alternatives can generate provider margins while imposing drug and financial toxicity on patients.
qs: Oncology has recently become a target of PE investment, with approximately 10% of medical oncologists and 15% of radiation oncologists practicing in PE-owned clinics by 2022.
Because PE firms seek short-term financial returns, they may increase use of lucrative but low-value services.

kp.k: Five treatments operationalized low-value cancer care
kp.d: Based on prior literature and professional-society recommendations, the study assessed two non-recommended treatments—GCSF for low-risk chemotherapy and denosumab for castration sensitive prostate cancer—and three high-cost options with lower-cost alternatives: nab-paclitaxel rather than paclitaxel for breast or lung cancer, adding bevacizumab to carboplatin plus paclitaxel for ovarian cancer, and originator biologics rather than biosimilars. Each outcome was binary and observed once per patient within its sub-cohort; patients could contribute to multiple sub-cohorts.
qs: We examined five low-value cancer treatments based on prior literature and/or recommendations by professional societies: two non-recommended treatments and three high-cost treatments with lower-cost alternatives (Table S1).
Each outcome was binary and observed only once for each patient.
Patients could be included in multiple sub-cohorts if they met the requirements of each;

kp.k: Medicare data captured acquisitions and treatment exposure
kp.d: The study used 100% traditional Medicare claims and Medicare Advantage national encounter data from 2015 through 2021, restricting MA records to contracts with highly complete data. Beneficiaries had new cancer diagnoses from January 1, 2016 to June 30, 2020, at least a one-year cancer diagnosis/treatment washout, and continuous specified coverage. The sample comprised 141,223 patients and 201,348 observations; sub-cohorts ranged from 9,609 denosumab observations to 72,476 biologics observations. PE exposure increased from 1.9% (584 of 31,236) in 2016 to 3.3% (1,154 of 34,696) in 2020. Exposure linked assigned oncologists’ historical addresses to acquisition records and dates.
qs: We used 100% traditional Medicare (TM) claims and Medicare Advantage (MA) national encounter data from 2015 through 2021.
The study comprised 141,223 patients contributing 201,348 observations (Figure S1, Table S3).
Physicians’ historical practice addresses were then mapped to those identified as PE-acquired (data from Pitchbook and other public sources, including press releases).

kp.d: The authors estimated each treatment separately using two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences with staggered exposure initiation, calendar-year and tax identification number fixed effects, and patient and community covariates. Exposure depended on whether the oncologist practiced at a PE-acquired address at the patient’s index diagnosis. Adjusted baseline differences between ever-exposed and never-exposed groups were not statistically significant for any treatment, and control and pre-intervention trends were not statistically different.
qs: We used a two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences (DID) model, accommodating staggered exposure initiation dates

Comparing patients treated by oncologists who ever vs. never practiced at a PE-acquired address, the adjusted use of low-value treatment was not statistically different at baseline (the not-PE acquired period for the treatment group)
Control and pre-intervention trends were not statistically different (DID parallel trends assumption) (Figure S2).

kp.k: Acquisition showed no increased low-value prescribing
kp.d: Adjusted DID prevalence differences, in percentage points with 95% confidence intervals, were −2.8 (−5.5 to −0.2) for GCSF; +3.7 (−7.3 to 14.7) for denosumab; −0.7 (−3.9 to 1.5) for nab-paclitaxel; −6.5 (−12.5 to −0.4) for bevacizumab; and −2.9 (−6.0 to 0.2) for biologics. The authors identify statistically significant reductions for GCSF and bevacizumab, but no statistically significant differences for the other three treatments. Their overall conclusion concerns absence of an observed association with increased use, not proof that ownership has no effects.
qs: After multivariable adjustment from the DID estimation, the corresponding prevalence differences were: GCSF, −2.8%-points (−5.5 to −0.2); denosumab, +3.7%-points (−7.3 to 14.7); nab-paclitaxel, −0.7%-points (−3.9 to 1.5); bevacizumab, −6.5%-points (−12.5 to −0.4); biologics, −2.9%-points (−6.0 to 0.2) (Table 1).

PE acquisition was not associated with differences in use of three of the low-value treatments and was associated with reductions in two low-value treatments (GCSF for low-risk chemotherapy and bevacizumab for ovarian cancer).

kp.k: Sensitivity analyses broadly supported the main findings
kp.d: Results were similar when radiation oncologists were eligible for patient assignment and when TIN fixed effects were removed. Separate analyses of Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare beneficiaries yielded no consistent trends. These checks supplement, rather than eliminate, the study’s stated causal and generalizability limitations.
qs: Results were similar when including radiation oncologists and removing TIN fixed effects (Tables S9, S10).
There were no consistent trends when analyzing Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare beneficiaries separately (Table S11).

kp.k: Profitability may depend on mechanisms beyond prescribing
kp.d: The authors contrast their findings with the hypothesis that PE owners would increase revenue-generating low-value services before resale. They report evidence from other medical settings of consolidation, pricing and staff reductions as alternative profit mechanisms, but call for research to establish whether these operate in oncology acquisitions. They interpret reduced GCSF and bevacizumab use as further support for the possibility that increasing drug utilization is not a common firm strategy.
qs: Studies of non-oncology medical settings have found that PE firms may use other mechanisms besides direct involvement in care delivery – such as consolidation, pricing, and staff reductions – to increase profitability.
Further study is needed to assess whether these strategies are employed in oncology acquisitions as well.
For two low-value services (GCSF and bevacizumab), use appeared unexpectedly lower in PE-acquired firms, further supporting that increased drug utilization may not be a common firm strategy.

kp.k: Procedure volume may condition ownership effects
kp.d: The authors report contrasting prior ophthalmology research finding increased intravitreal injection volume and higher cost per procedure through substitution of more-expensive drugs after PE acquisition. They hypothesize that standardized, high-volume procedures offer greater revenue opportunities from drug substitution than the relatively uncommon oncology treatments examined here. This is a proposed explanation, not a mechanism tested by the study.
qs: PE-acquired ophthalmology practices had both increased volume of intravitreal injections and increased cost per procedure due to substitution of more-expensive drugs.

The difference may be that services such as intravitreal injections are standardized, high-volume procedures such that substituting higher-priced drugs might substantially impact overall practice revenue, whereas the five low-value treatments we studied are relatively uncommon and therefore less likely to receive attention by practice ownership.

kp.k: Scope and confounding limit causal interpretation
kp.d: The study examined only five treatments, not other services, and acknowledges potential bias from unmeasured confounders despite adjustment and DID comparisons. Small sample sizes prevented event-study analysis, leaving heterogeneous effects over time unassessed. Findings are limited to Medicare; the authors recommend studying commercially insured patients, whose reimbursement is typically greater.
qs: This study was limited to five low-value cancer treatments and did not analyze other services.
While we adjusted for patient and community-level factors, results may be biased by unmeasured confounders.
the finding may still be associative and may not imply causality.
Due to small sample sizes we were unable to conduct an event study analysis; this study therefore did not assess the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects over time.
Our results are limited to Medicare; future research should assess care delivery for commercially-insured patients, for whom reimbursement is typically greater.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mitchell and coauthors report that private equity ownership was not associated with increased use of five studied low-value cancer treatments. This is a healthcare ownership study, not a claim about AI or legal services.
pts.d: The authors find statistically significant reductions in GCSF use for low-risk chemotherapy and addition of bevacizumab for ovarian cancer, and no statistically significant differences for denosumab, nab-paclitaxel, or originator biologics with biosimilar alternatives. They distinguish this finding from their motivating hypothesis that PE firms' pursuit of short-term returns might encourage lucrative low-value care. They suggest, without establishing, that oncology owners may pursue profitability through mechanisms other than increased drug utilization, and that the selected treatments may be too uncommon to attract ownership attention.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The findings rest on Medicare claims and encounter data analyzed using a two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences model.
pts.d: The sample comprised 141,223 patients contributing 201,348 observations. The authors linked oncologists' historical addresses to PE acquisitions identified through Pitchbook and public sources, then compared changes associated with PE exposure against clinicians never exposed to PE. Models adjusted for patient and community characteristics and included calendar-year and tax-identification-number fixed effects. Adjusted differences were −2.8 percentage points for GCSF (95% CI −5.5 to −0.2), +3.7 for denosumab (−7.3 to 14.7), −0.7 for nab-paclitaxel (−3.9 to 1.5), −6.5 for bevacizumab (−12.5 to −0.4), and −2.9 for biologics (−6.0 to 0.2). Sensitivity analyses including radiation oncologists or removing practice fixed effects produced similar results; separate Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare analyses showed no consistent trends. The proposed alternative profitability mechanisms draw on prior non-oncology studies rather than direct evidence from this study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern historical Medicare care, not a future prediction, and are explicitly limited in scope and causal interpretation.
pts.d: Published online on 30 March 2026, the study uses 2015–2021 data for beneficiaries newly diagnosed from January 1, 2016 through June 30, 2020. Eligibility required a cancer-free washout of at least one year and continuous specified Medicare coverage; Medicare Advantage contracts were selected for highly complete encounter records. PE exposure was assigned according to the oncologist's practice ownership at the patient's diagnosis date. The authors restrict conclusions to five treatments and Medicare patients, acknowledge possible unmeasured confounding, and caution that the associations may not be causal. Small samples prevented an event study, leaving heterogeneous effects over time unassessed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied populations are Medicare cancer patients and their oncology practices, with implications for prescribing incentives under PE ownership.
pts.d: Treatment-specific cohorts encompass patients receiving low-risk chemotherapy, patients with castration-sensitive prostate cancer, patients with breast or lung cancer, patients receiving carboplatin plus paclitaxel for ovarian cancer, and patients eligible for biologics with biosimilar alternatives. The authors describe low-value treatment as a source of avoidable spending, drug toxicity, and financial toxicity, but the measured outcomes are treatment receipt rather than direct changes in costs or patient health. PE-owned practices and their investors are discussed as potentially responding to revenue incentives. Commercially insured patients are outside the study's demonstrated scope.
